What pass requires: The target standard appears as the full standard text in the lesson plan header — a complete standard statement, not a bare code, an abbreviation, or a paraphrase. Wherever the standard is restated in any artifact, the wording matches the header word-for-word. Pass = full text in header and consistent verbatim usage throughout. Fail = code-only citation, paraphrase, or wording that drifts between header and body.

A prior standard or explicitly named prerequisite concept is identified with enough specificity that a teacher knows what prior knowledge to check. Pass = a named standard code (e.g., '3.NF.1') or a specific skill description (e.g., 'students can solve result-unknown addition within 20'). Fail = vague reference (e.g., 'students should have some background in fractions').

Criterion: Learning goal separates Big Idea from SWBAT
What pass requires: The lesson distinguishes between an enduring understanding (Big Idea) and specific observable student behaviors (SWBAT - students will be able to"). Pass = two distinct components. Fail = one merged statement like 'students will learn about fractions'."
At least 3 misconceptions or anticipated challenges are named. Pass = 3 or more entries. Fail = fewer than 3.

Criterion: Anticipated challenges — each entry is complete
What pass requires: Each challenge entry names (a) what students do, (b) why it happens, and (c) a specific teacher move. Pass = all three components present in every entry. Fail = any entry is missing a component, or teacher moves are generic ('re-teach', 'check for understanding').

Criterion: Lesson phases present and sequenced correctly
What pass requires: The lesson has a recognizable instructional arc appropriate to the domain with time allocations on each phase. Pass = all required phases present with times. Fail = phases missing, merged, or unlabeled.
At least 3 look-fors are named for the main practice or work phase. Pass = 3 or more entries. Fail = fewer than 3.

Criterion: Look-fors — each entry describes observable student behavior
What pass requires: Each look-for describes a specific observable student behavior — what the teacher is watching for — explains why it matters, and gives a teacher move. Additionally, FIRST classify the anchor task yourself: does it genuinely admit multiple correct responses (e.g., several valid equations or interpretations can fit)? Only if it does, the look-fors must also include explicit guidance that multiple correct responses can match the anchor task; if the anchor has a single correct answer this requirement is waived — do NOT fail for missing multi-correct guidance. State your classification in the explanation. Fail = any look-for reads as a teacher instruction ('circulate and check for understanding') rather than an observable student behavior, or required multi-correct guidance is absent.

Visual or representational choices are pedagogically informed WITH stated rationale — e.g., a drawing-first option, an intentional choice not to pre-print a diagram, or guidance on when to introduce a visual model and why. Pass = at least one visual or representational choice with explicit reasoning. Fail = visuals appear without rationale, or no visual/representational thinking is evident in the plan.

At least one task is designed to generate genuine student curiosity or interest — an unexpected or novel context, an open-ended question, a real-world scenario students would care about, or productive-struggle design. A generic word problem or comprehension task does not count; there must be a deliberate hook. Not every task needs this quality — one is sufficient.

The work assigned in each phase is plausibly completable in the allotted minutes by students at this grade level. Count the tasks in each phase and estimate minutes per task. Pass = every phase's workload fits its time. Fail = any phase assigns clearly more work than its time allows (e.g., 12 problems in a 20-minute block that also includes discussion). Judge the pace of this room: students who read at a 3rd-5th grade level, with processing supports.

Criterion: At least one task demands student reasoning
What pass requires: A student who only memorizes or follows steps cannot complete at least one task. Pass = one or more tasks require explanation, justification, comparison, or argumentation. Fail = every task is recall or procedural with a single right answer.

Criterion: Exit ticket targets the hardest case
What pass requires: The exit ticket targets the structurally hardest version of the standard — not the easiest. FIRST determine the standard's structurally hardest case yourself (e.g., start-unknown for operations word problems, counterclaim handling for argument writing, mechanism-level reasoning for explanatory models). THEN classify the exit-ticket task: quote it and state which case or demand it targets. Pass only if the two match. Show both classifications in the explanation.

The student-facing worksheet itself includes at least one prompt inviting student reasoning or choice: a self-assessment question, a reflection prompt, an open-ended extension, or a 'show/explain your thinking' prompt attached to a task (these count even when embedded in task items). Teacher-led discussion prompts in the lesson plan do NOT count. Judge the student materials only.

Criterion: Student materials contain no teacher-only content
What pass requires: Student-facing materials contain no teacher-only content: no look-fors, no misconception or points-of-difficulty notes, no assessment rationale, no answer keys, no instructions directed at the teacher ('the teacher places…', 'circulate and…'), no stage directions written TO the teacher ('Show…', 'Display…', 'Read aloud…', 'Distribute…'), and no third-person narration of student activity ('Students work in pairs…', 'Students blend the sounds…'). Scaffolding addressed TO STUDENTS in second person (hints, 'Remember:' reminders, sentence frames, worked examples) is student content and is fine — do NOT fail for it. Judge the student materials only; content in the lesson plan or observation sheet is irrelevant here.

Criterion: Lesson plan is concise and scannable
What pass requires: The lesson plan in the chat message is scannable: the agenda, the blocks and the answer key are findable at a glance, and the whole plan fits on a screen or two. Pass = a teacher can find the next action within 10 seconds. Fail = rationale and actions run together, or the plan sprawls past two screens.
Notes: Changed: the plan lives in the chat, not a document.

Criterion: Teacher and student materials describe the same tasks
What pass requires: The student materials' tasks ARE the same tasks the lesson plan describes — same contexts, same numbers and specifics, same count — and the observation sheet's look-fors are the ones the lesson plan names. Direction 1: every activity named in the plan has a corresponding student-facing version. Direction 2: nothing in the student materials is unaccounted for in the plan. List every mismatch found; pass only if BOTH directions are clean.

The lesson plan includes one or two brief rationale notes identifying which elements must be PRESERVED to maintain alignment and rigor (non-negotiables such as curriculum sequence, grade-level demand, discourse structure) and why. Generic praise ('this lesson is well-structured') does not count.

Misconceptions, look-fors, and prerequisite references are specific to this standard's content — a reader could not transplant them unchanged to an unrelated topic. The standard text quoted in body text matches the header word-for-word wherever it appears. Fail = boilerplate misconceptions ('students may get confused'), generic look-fors, or a standard subtly reworded between header and body.
Contexts, names, numbers, grade level, and timing references agree across all artifacts. No artifact narrates a context, example, or task that the others do not have. Judge all artifacts together.
No conflicting counts, durations, units, instructions, or directions between any two artifacts. Quote any contradiction found in the explanation.

The plan never contradicts itself about which task or case is hardest; discussion and closing phases anchor on the case the rationale identifies as most important; and any task types the prose promises (e.g., 'students will work start-unknown problems') actually exist in the materials. Fail = the plan promises content that never appears, or different sections disagree about emphasis.

Every concept, case, or notation appearing in the synthesis/closing phase was investigated by students in an earlier phase. Nothing appears for the first time in the closing. Fail = the summary introduces a case, term, or representation students never worked with.

Artifacts favor structure over prose: paragraphs stay within roughly 3 sentences; parallel content (per-group supports, per-phase variants, look-fors) appears in tables or bullet lists rather than stacked multi-sentence paragraphs; bullets are one-idea fragments rather than chained clauses. Fail = any wall-of-text paragraph or parallel variants written as back-to-back prose paragraphs.

Every student-facing prompt that demands written work (problems, exit ticket, reflection) is followed by visible blank writing space proportionate to the expected response and grade level — younger students get more room, multi-sentence answers get generous space, fill-in items get a line or two. Fail = any prompt with no adjacent writing space or space plainly too small for the expected response.

The target standard's full text appears exactly once (header or standards callout). Prerequisite and forward standards are referenced by code plus a short gist, never pasted in full. Fail = the full target standard repeated elsewhere, or prerequisite/forward standard text quoted verbatim.

After delivering the lesson plan, the model offers at least two meaningful follow-up options (e.g., differentiation, multi-lingual learner layer, state-specific adaptation). Pass = two or more specific options. Fail = none, or options are generic ('let me know if you want changes').

Criterion: No curriculum-specific terminology for non-curriculum teachers
What pass requires: For teachers who did not indicate they use a named curriculum (IM etc.): the lesson plan contains no proprietary terminology from a specific program. Pass = no curriculum-specific language for teachers without that curriculum signal. Fail = any curriculum-proprietary term appears in output for a teacher who didn't indicate that curriculum.

If the teacher confirmed IM: lesson uses the Launch → Explore → Discuss → Synthesize structure with IM routine names. If another curriculum is named: the lesson matches that curriculum's instructional model. If no curriculum is named: any coherent research-based structure passes — a generic four-phase arc is fine and is NOT a violation — so long as no curriculum-proprietary terminology appears. Fail = IM terminology for a non-IM teacher, or a named curriculum's instructional model ignored.

Math misconceptions must name the wrong equation form vs. the correct one (e.g., 'student writes 45 + ? = 18 instead of 45 − 18 = ?'), not describe a general confusion pattern. Pass = at least 2 of 3 misconceptions include a specific wrong form. Fail = all misconceptions are general pattern descriptions.

Criterion: Problem set covers the standard's structural variety
What pass requires: FIRST enumerate the structural cases of the target standard yourself (e.g., unknown positions for operations word problems, transformation types, proportional vs. non-proportional cases). THEN verify every enumerated case appears in the practice problems or exit ticket. List the enumeration and where each case appears in the explanation. Fail = any structural case of the standard is absent from the problem set.

Each student task's answer surface fits its activity: a task asking students to compute, draw, partition, or build a model gets open space or the diagram itself; a task asking for a composed sentence or explanation may use ruled lines at any grade. Fail = ruled writing lines under a task whose expected work is drawing or computation. Judge the student materials only; name the mismatched task in the explanation.

Criterion: Three-dimensional learning targets are separate and explicit
What pass requires: The lesson states three distinct learning targets: one for science & engineering practices (what students will practice), one for disciplinary core ideas (what students will understand), one for crosscutting concepts (which crosscutting concept students will apply). Pass = three distinct bullets, each labeled with the dimension. Fail = one merged objective, or DCI-only targets.

Criterion: Phenomenon is observable and drives the lesson
What pass requires: The anchoring phenomenon is something students can directly observe or is a specific real-world event (9–12). It is posed as a question to explain, not as an illustration of a concept the teacher will then explain. Pass = phenomenon is specific and students are positioned as sense-makers. Fail = phenomenon is abstract, described rather than experienced, or used as a hook before teacher explanation.

Criterion: CCC is named and used by students not just cited in the plan
What pass requires: A specific crosscutting concept (Patterns, Cause and Effect, Energy and Matter, etc.) is named in the lesson and students are required to use it explicitly — in their claim/evidence/reasoning writing, model, or discussion. Pass = CCC named and required in student output. Fail = CCC mentioned in teacher plan but students are never asked to apply it.

Criterion: Model revision is present and mechanistic
What pass requires: Students draw or update an explanatory model that shows how and why (mechanism), not just what (label). Model is revised based on evidence gathered in the lesson. Pass = model revision task present and described as mechanistic. Fail = model is a labeled diagram that predates the investigation, or no model revision step.

The claim/evidence/reasoning writing task requires students to cite specific evidence from the investigation (data, observations) — not from prior knowledge or the internet. Pass = prompt specifies 'from the investigation' or equivalent. Fail = students could write the CER without doing the investigation.

Criterion: Quantitative reasoning required in student analysis
What pass requires: For 6–12 standards with quantitative data: students must use numbers (not just qualitative descriptions) in their claims or explanations. Pass = at least one task requires numerical evidence or mathematical modeling. Fail = all analysis is qualitative when the data is quantitative.
Notes: Only applies to Gr 6–12 standards with quantitative data

Criterion: Grade-level demand is maintained by the end
What pass requires: The standard's hardest case appears, unsimplified, in the last task every student does and in the closing. Supports before that point (friendly numbers first, word banks, starters, worked examples) are access, not a reduced task. Pass = the hardest case is reached by everyone. Fail = the hardest case never appears, or appears only in an optional part (b).
Notes: Changed for a modified curriculum: demand is judged at the end of the arc, not at every step.

Criterion: Standard's full numerical scope is used by the end
What pass requires: The lesson may open with friendly numbers, but the last item every student does uses the standard's full numerical scope (decimals or fractions when the standard says rational numbers; the whole range when it gives one). Pass = the final common item meets the scope. Fail = no item every student does reaches it.
Notes: Changed from upstream, where starting with friendly numbers fails. In an SDC room friendly numbers first is sound practice; what matters is that the real numbers arrive.

What pass requires: Students gather data or observations before the lesson gives the scientific explanation. Short explicit instruction on vocabulary, safety, tools, or procedure may come first; the explanation of the phenomenon may not. Pass = no part of the mechanism is told before students have their own evidence. Fail = the explanation comes first.
Notes: Changed: explicit instruction before the investigation is allowed when it teaches how to investigate, not what will be found.

What pass requires: The package is a lesson plan written in the chat, a student packet, and a slide deck (or only the parts the teacher asked for). Pass = every requested part is present. Fail = a requested part is missing.
Notes: Changed: a plan in the chat counts as the lesson plan. Upstream asked for a document.

What pass requires: The lesson names at least two moments of student-to-student talk, whatever the period's length. Each has a named move, a question worth talking about, a sentence stem, and a job for the listener. At least one runs on a talk slide; a game round run as talk (partners agree on a timer first) counts as one. No minimum minutes. Pass = two or more complete talk moves. Fail = fewer, or a move without its question, stem, or listener's job.
Notes: Replaces upstream P-M3's ten-minute Discuss rule, and applies to science too.

What pass requires: The student-facing English (prompts, directions, notes) reads at or below the profile's reading level, no sentence runs past 20 words, and long words outside the key vocabulary are rare. Pass = the renderer's report shows the grade at or under target with no unaddressed long sentence. Fail = any long sentence, or a grade more than one above target.
Notes: Upstream has no readability or student-experience criterion. Key words count as easy because they are being taught.

What pass requires: Three to six key words are named for the lesson. Each is highlighted wherever it appears on the packet and the slides, has a word slide (the word, how to say it, a photograph or diagram, its language line), and is used in at least one task. Pass = all of that for every key word. Fail = a key word unmarked, without a word slide, or never used.

The packet fits its budget (two pages for a 60-minute lesson; a block aims for two, never more than four; an even count), every page is at least three-quarters full, and every task prints whole: no prompt is ever on a different page from its answer space, here or in Google Docs. Pass = check_packet.py reports clean. Fail = any error.
Notes: Student experience on paper, measured rather than judged.

Criterion: One short line per home language
What pass requires: Every question and direction, on the packet and on the slides, carries one line per home language in the profile, no longer than the English it supports. Scaffolding (stems, examples, headings, captions) stays English. Pass = no missing or long line reported, and the lines say the task. Fail = a missing line, a doubled page, or a line that doesn't say the task.
Notes: Upstream treats language support as all or nothing.

Criterion: Accommodations built in from the first draft
What pass requires: Every accommodation ticked in the profile is present in the first materials delivered, and the plan's Differentiation line names each one and where it landed. Pass = all ticked items present and named. Fail = one missing, or added only after the teacher asked.
Notes: Feedback: IEP and 504 supports arrived as revisions.

What pass requires: The lesson makes at least one move for engagement, one for representation, and one for action and expression, drawn from the profile's UDL checklist when it has one; the plan names all three and each is visible in the packet or the deck. Pass = three named and present. Fail = any principle missing.
Notes: Replaces upstream O5, which passed with any two strategies.

Criterion: The deck runs the same lesson
What pass requires: Every packet task appears on a slide in the packet's own words, with the packet page named; the deck checker reports no errors; every photograph argues for the claim on its slide. Pass = all three. Fail = a task missing from the slides, different wording, a checker error, or a photograph that only matches the topic.

Each game round is a fair guess (a student could reason toward it without already knowing it), its reveal explains in a sentence a student could repeat, and its answer, and every sort card's bin, agrees with the packet's answer key. Pass = every game meets all three. Fail = any one.

Criterion: The whole plan is in the chat
What pass requires: The chat message carries the full plan: objective with standard, agenda summing to the period, the blocks with say-aloud lines and three look-fors, the talk moves, media, differentiation (accommodations, language, UDL), at least three predicted errors with why and the move, the answer key, the closing check, and what to keep if time is cut. Pass = all present. Fail = any missing.
Notes: The judge reads the plan from the chat. Upstream judges only attached documents and fails a lean, chat-first plan.

What pass requires: The response names the previous lesson it built from (found in the working folder or Drive), the do-now reaches back to it, and the Day map row and class notes are updated, or handed over where there is no folder. Pass = all three. Fail = any one missing.
Notes: Feedback: yesterday's lesson had to be re-uploaded by hand.
